Madam Speaker, this is a very complex series of bills and I am not going to attempt to define any particular part of the bill. I do want to make a few remarks because banks are not giving Canadians the kind of service which they should be able to expect.
Most Canadians hope that the next time the Bank Act is brought up and reviewed some of the power of the banks will be curtailed. They hope that the small entrepreneur, homeowner, farmer, small businessman, or simply someone who owns a home can be sure they will not be put in as great a disadvantage in dealing with the bank as in the past.
There is no doubt in the eyes of the public in Canada that the banks are seen to be almost in a position where they are unassailable. Consequently the person dealing with them feels very weak and unable to deal with these large corporations.

Government Orders
Does this series of bills allow the small entrepreneur, the small businessman or the farmer to feel more confidence in dealing with financial institutions? The answer is patently no. It does not.
Possibly, as suggested in these bills, there is a need to rearrange or restructure the whole financial system. Maybe it all needs to be reviewed. However, the aim of the review should be the empowerment of the people who use these institutions not to increase the powers of the financial institutions.
We all want and need financial institutions which are secure. These bills do not in my mind, or in the minds of people who have looked at them thoroughly, ensure that there will be no further financial disasters affecting the small depositor or the small entrepreneur.
These bills are part of a corporate agenda, or I could say possibly a Conservative agenda, which puts the economy more into the hands of the financial institutions than it is right now. For instance, if someone wanted to start farming-although that might be a bad example because at the moment only a fool would get himself involved in farming-or start a small business, they would borrow the money. The idea is that they should be able to pay back the money and make some profit on it.
The only institution that is guaranteed a profit from the person's efforts is not them-because they are working hard at it or are a good manager-but the bank or the financial institution which has the security of return. It gets everything if they miss a payment.
As I said, farming is not a good example-and during the present recession even a small business is not a good example-but the same situation can be outlined in almost any entrepreneurial venture. Only the money lender gets anything out of it.
The financial institutions which are supposed to be the pillars of our economy are not helping our economy. In most cases they are leeching off the entrepreneurial efforts and work of the people who are trying to make a living.
This government's solution in these bills has been to undermine the traditional pillars, to reduce the number of players and put in place a few megafinancial supermarkets which will then have more and more power in more and more areas of the financial world.
From experience, this would seem similar to what happened in the grocery business. We used to have lots of grocery stores around, small enterprises which worked well and provided a living for the people who operated them. We now have supermarkets which have eliminated all these small and efficient operations. These have been eliminated.
The same thing is happening in farming. The larger and sometimes less efficient operator is gradually eliminating the smaller operator, which is a living for many people. The government is also doing in this case what it has already done to the airline industry. It has deregulated it so that size becomes the main instrument of success, not service, not how well the company serves people, not what it has done to help the economy. The size of the institution is the basis of its success.
Deregulation means legal requirements and constraints are deleted or substantially loosened on a particular venture. This allows and works toward greater reliance on corporate self-regulation and good will.
Actually, what it does foster is some kind of a corporate tyranny. As the corporation gets bigger, has its fingers in more pies, and covers more of the structure of the financial world, it is able to affect our economy and each of us much more than it has in the past. Turning to a large organization which has a dominance in its particular field, there is a recognition that in many cases the larger the corporation the less efficient it becomes. Because these corporations are large and have a considerable amount of power, the cost of these inefficiencies is then charged to the consumer. They get away with it because there are no corporations in place to compete.
Financial institutions do not have an unblemished record of purity. In fact, from the experience of failure over the past few years of trust companies and banks, we know that conflict of interests and self-dealing have been the common reason for the failure of some of those institutions. It seems very logical that the projected structure will further exacerbate this situation so the possibility of misuse of the financial instruments becomes more likely and less detectable with fewer regulations, larger institutions, blurred areas of responsibility, and unclear ownership requirements. This opens up the possibility of self-interest being covered up when it is
October 2, 1991

much more difficult to examine the operations of the institutions. They are not required by law to present before the public their methods of operation.
I question the global competition which the banks, trust companies and insurance companies say is so important for them to survive. Is it so important to our economy? Is it important to the individual on the street? Is it important to us when we insure our car or house? Is it important to the majority of Canadians?
After all, good government is possible only with the consent of the majority. The majority of people should be served by changes to these institutions. We suggest that this is not entirely what is happening.
These bills are going to committee. I hope the committees will look at them and change them so that they will protect the consumer, the client, and the small entrepreneur from the financial institutions, instead of the other way around. I hope that the committees will look at these bills and ensure that what happens in these bills-the changes made to the institutions, the allowing of the relationship between these institutions-protects the consumer, protects the small entrepreneur, and protects the individuals who use them most and does not allow these institutions to take unfair advantage.
My father used to go to the city and say: "I wonder why it is that all the big buildings in this city are owned by the banks or the insurance companies. It must be because they take more out of our pockets than anybody else does". I think he still thinks that is true. The government has a responsibility to protect the general consumer from that kind of situation.
The effect of the changes in the Bank Act the last few times has been to provide less protection than before. As a farmer I know, for instance, that there was a time when if I bought a combine the only collateral required for that combine was the combine itself. Five years later the Bank Act was changed so that the collateral could be the combine and anything I produced on my farm.
Under the present Bank Act if I fail to pay, the bank or the financial corporation can take my combine, anything I produce and my land. That is the kind of change that has happened in the last few bank acts. It gives less and less protection to the people who need it the most. It
Government Orders
gives protection to the people who have the power: the corporations.
The size of the institution is not as important as security. It is not as important as supervision. It is not as important as the government deciding to do what is best. We should not be changing these acts to protect the financial corporations or make it possible for them to make more profits. We should be changing these acts to ensure that the economy and the individuals who drive the economy are protected from large corporations which do not have, in our experience, a great many scruples when it comes to dealing with people.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to put a couple of comments on the record during the closing moments of second reading of these bills that are before the House.
I was thinking that perhaps the most important consideration that the House of Commons should make in dealing with the Bank Act and dealing with financial institutions is the consideration of the effect of the Bank Act on Canadians, and I mean ordinary Canadians.
I was dealing with a problem just the other day where people who were laid off from a mining operation in the community of Buchans in Newfoundland found themselves in the situation where the separation pay that they had received, their pension funds, all of a sudden were being deducted from their federal government cheques, their MYLAP cheques.
What had happened was this: The federal government had passed a law that said those funds could no longer be rolled in RRSPs. Those people out there who had been laid off from the company, they didn't know anything about that. They did not know. Then of course the banks and the insurance companies said that ignorance of the law is no excuse, and neither is it. They were informed
October 2, 1991

after several months that what they had to do was put those funds into a trust fund.
The insurance companies and the banks did not inform them of what had transpired in the House of Commons that affected the moneys being sent out by the insurance companies to the banks. In other words, nobody thought to have a look at those people whom they were supposed to be serving as banks, as financial institutions, to point out to them that a simple change could have saved them an awful lot of money.
Well now, of course, it is too late. Those funds are gone. I know it is a bit complicated. It is difficult to simplify it even in speaking to the people concerned, but believe me there should have been a mechanism which said that the insurance companies and the banks involved had to inform those people that the law had changed and of the way to arrange things financially so that they would not be penalized.
Members stood up in this House not too long ago from the province of British Columbia. They were complaining about the fact that the banks were sending out letters to fishermen in that province about the moneys that were owed under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act which came to an end in this Chamber a couple of years ago. In other words, when they get a loan now it is under the Small Businesses Loans Act.
The same letters that were received by those fishermen in the province of British Columbia were received by the fishermen in the province of Quebec on the north shore. The same letters were received in the province of New Brunswick, in the province of Nova Scotia, in the province of Prince Edward Island, and in the province of Newfoundland.
What it was was this: the banks had sent a letter to each person who had defaulted on loans eight and ten years ago that were guaranteed by the federal government and for which all collection proceedings had gone ahead. They had lost perhaps their boats, their nets, or whatever was put up as collateral. The banks were writing a letter on behalf of the federal Department of Finance to collect money on behalf of the federal government.
Government Orders
What a cosy relationship that was. Was there a finder's fee? They were acting as a collection agency. Were they getting paid? No, they were not. They were not getting paid. They were not being given a finder's fee. They paid for the stamp that went to every single person who had defaulted eight and ten years ago on loans telling them that the federal government wanted them to pay up on the money that it had paid to the banks because the federal government had guaranteed the loan in the first place. What a cosy relationship, a relationship that should not be there, that these acts of Parliament should prohibit.
I suppose we are getting into a new age, an age where transactions are not done with cash, not done with cheques, not done with money any more, but done with banking cards. I noticed the other day that the federal government has embarked on an experimental program with the banks in Canada to issue people who are receiving unemployment insurance benefits with a card, a banking card, with a 97K memory, whatever that means. The individual would be able to go to a bank and, instead of going into an unemployment insurance office and filling out forms or mailing forms in, they would be able to utilize a machine in the bank that would give them credit on this card.
Two cities are now being selected to try out this new system of disbursing money to individuals through the unemployment insurance scheme. Of course it requires the co-operation of banks because the banks would operate the machine and a credit would be registered when the individual used that card. They are calling it the smart card. That to my way of thinking was devised by some computer whiz somewhere in a federal government agency for people to use cards where there are no banking machines.
How many banking machines are there in our high unemployment areas of Canada? The Privacy Commissioner has looked at this experiment, given it his okay, and said that as long as the rest of the memory on the card is not being used for other purposes or is not an invasion of privacy into a person's bank account, then it is okay to use it.
I have spent many years in this Chamber. I have spent many of those years dealing with problems associated with people getting money and then having to pay it back after the fact, back to this federal government.

I can tell you now, Mr. Speaker, that the number of problems associated with people filling out that unemployment insurance form is going to multiply, because now somebody will be expected to go with a card into a bank and on that card will be their credit. They can then take that card and use it as a credit card anywhere in our society, based on what? Based on the information that was fed into a computer.
The minister who approved that of course is the Minister of Employment and Immigration. I have one final bit of advice for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Instead of issuing smart cards to unemployed people, we should be issuing a get smart card to the Minister of Employment and Immigration.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should defer to the hon. member from the city of Toronto on the basis that I could probably learn quite a bit from him and therefore raise the level of erudition of the speech I am about to make.
Anyway, what we have here is the continuation of the whole corporate agenda which we saw exposed in its whole rotten being most vividly on election day, as someone has already indicated, November 21, 1988. Can you think of a more important day or a more significant day for the American non-banks to be able to come into Canada and operate as banks?
What we have here is a corporate agenda in spades, starting on November 21, 1988, election day. Shame on the government for having done it at least in the western part of Canada which is sometimes a problem with us. It established a mandate to do so simply on the basis of an Order in Council from the government of the previous election and continued on as arrogantly from that time into this time. Experience has shown us since that time that what came forth so vividly on election day was the beginning of a series of tragedies for Canada.
We have the experience of the free trade deal, which is the over-all deregulation, the umbrella deregulation scheme for the corporate agenda, having been hived off in the intervening time in Parliament through deregulation of airlines and trucking and, of course, changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, where the government is no longer involved. Of course we need to have a level playing field and that would be so unfair to our poor American cousins south of the border. It would
constitute an unfair trading practice vis-a-vis our commercial trading and financial dealings with them.
Let us look at one example of deregulation that has still not been completed. Maybe we should refer to a couple of them, airlines and trucking. Airline deregulation is not complete yet. It would certainly surprise me, hearing the rumblings coming from across the House, if the American airlines are not granted cabotage, which means they could bring passengers into Canada from the United States. There are so few American airlines of course, compared to Canadian ones. I should not even say that. It has come to the point where you cannot make any kind of a joke in this House for fear it is taken the wrong way.
Of course there are many more airlines in the United States and of course they are going to be bringing passengers in here and once cabotage is allowed, they are going to be demanding it. Any sort of limitation on our part is going to be strongly resisted, no longer by the government of the United States. The American airlines will be pleased enough to carry that on for Carla Hills and Company on their own.
Unfortunately when we hear rumours with regard to what has happened in Canada with deregulation, they usually come true. The rumours are that in all probability, one and perhaps even both of Canada's airlines may simply disappear from commerce in Canada.
The rumblings of Air Canada making some kind of an arrangement with one of the American airlines, U.S. Air, I think, is certainly disconcerting.
Without belabouring the point and referring to the trucking industry, we all are very well aware of the demonstrations late last spring and early summer of the Canadian truckers. They came to Ottawa to tiy to make representations to Parliament and to the opposition. They got a good reception from us but received a very negative reception from the government. Of course they had to repeat their actions within the last week or two in order to tiy to get the government's attention insofar as their plight is concerned.
I heard a reference in the House but I am not sure if it was in Question Period or not, just in the last couple of days, that 60 per cent of cross-border trucking was still carried on by Canadian truckers. Those are certainly old figures because it has almost turned entirely around -60 per cent of the cross-border trucking used to be done by Canadian trucks, now it is the other way around. The number of Canadian trucks involved in cross-border
October 2, 1991

trucking is diminishing very, very rapidly. The last figure I heard was 60-40 in favour of the Americans.
The point is this. We have this experience as far as deregulation is concerned in other industries and there is no reason why we should have any confidence in this government or in anything they do as far as helping Canadian business, industry or financial services are concerned. Speaking of those institutions themselves, I realize they were talking here about banking and financial institutions. The Canadian financial institutions are ostensibly heavily regulated even now and look at the changes to the Bank Act as being something which deregulates them and provides for less regulation. The experience of the Canadian financial institution is bad enough. It does not matter whether you think of the banks and their extremely high and atrocious rates of interest they charge on their credit cards. The rates they charge on bank credit cards are usurious. For what it is worth, I guess we ought to give the finance ministers a bit of credit for having brought the interest rate down as much as they have. But we also ought to really get on the case of the finance ministers as we were, and on this finance minister, for not doing everything he can to bring the interest rates which those financial institutions charge the Canadian consumer down.
We have the atrocious example out west, and I know there are examples in the east, of Principal Trust that is provincially and federally regulated. Those people who put their trust in Principal Trust have suffered enormous financial loss.
We are going to deregulate. This will not only eventually affect Canadian institutions, but if American Express is any example, American institutions which find their way into Canada as well. I am sure there are other financial institutions in the states which would take great exception, umbrage even, at not being able to come into Canada as American Express has done.
We could go on and on. There is a tremendous amount of danger in the banks getting into the insurance business. We do not have any problems with banks selling insurance for other companies if they, in their branches, want to sell for the Co-operator's, the Sask Mutual Insurance, or whatever and why not Saskatchewan government insurance as well. That is fine. But for banks to own the insurance company is something which would be absolutely intolerable.

Those kinds of examples can go on and on. We have the example of Eaton's and The Bay having joint financial services, which seems to be a bit of a conflict of interest in itself. We would certainly be at a great disadvantage as Canadians if, in addition to that, they were also able to form a trust company and then form a bank. It seems to me that what we would eventually have is a coming together of almost all the financial institutions in the country, whatever their shape or form, into one. That is the main danger and something we have to guard against.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague from Saskatoon has talked about the problems which our legislation at this stage presents with respect to regulating foreign banks. I want to talk very briefly about the case of one of the most serious gaps which has been demonstrated by the case of the Bank of Credit and Commerce Canada.
The Bank of Credit and Commerce Canada, or BCCI Canada as I am going to refer to it, is of course the Canadian branch of the large international bank which became noted, to quote a CIA memorandum from 1986, as the "Bank of Crooks and Criminals". It was a bank which operated throughout the world in a way which is now quite clear in retrospect, was fraudulent virtually from the bottom up.
It was a bank which has now been charged in the United States in a number of different jurisdictions with fraudulently controlling American banks in states where it had been refused a bank licence itself. It has been identified as the bank of choice for money laundering by those engaged in drug dealing and other criminal activities throughout the world.
BCCI, in short, is an example of the worst excesses of the capitalist system world-wide. BCCI operated here in Canada through a series of eight bank branches across this country. It did so despite the fact that the Canadian Bankers' Association wrote formally to the Superintendent of Financial Institutions and spoke informally on a number of occasions before that to the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, suggesting that this was a bank which because of its associations and its reputations

Government Orders
throughout the world, did not have any right to be able to operate as a bank here in this country.
You might think, Mr. Speaker, that this was an unusual event for the CBA to take such a position. We asked the Canadian Bankers' Association in fact on Monday night if it had ever taken such a position before with respect to a member institution of its association. The answer: "No, we have never taken such a position."
They took that position in 1984 having communicated the position verbally before 1984 and despite that, the regulators in this country did nothing to stop that bank's operations in Canada. We also heard testimony on Monday night which indicated that RCMP investigations had taken place with reference to this bank in 1988 and
1989.
These RCMP investigations had led the officers involved to communicate with the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, OSFI, and had led those officers to tell OSFI of certain activities which they had discovered with respect to BCCI. Nothing happened. Nothing happened to stop this bank from continuing to receive deposits.
This bank was finally closed down on July 5 of this year, not because of something that emerged in Canada but because of international action co-ordinated by the Bank of England. The $107 million in deposits was immediately frozen for those depositors in this country who had relied on the regulation which was being undertaken of this bank.
Of that $107 million in deposits, only $20 million was covered by deposit insurance. That money has gone back to depositors, the $20 million.
That leaves something in the order of $87 million which depositors in good faith put into this bank and have very little chance of obtaining.
You might ask what this has to do with the bills in front of us. When the Canadian Bankers' Association testified before us on Monday night at the Standing Committee on Finance, it made a direct connection to Bill C-19, the revisions to the Bank Act. It indicates that there is no reference, and I am quoting here directly from the Canadian Bankers' Association, in the current act to the required regulatory standards of a foreign bank applicant.
The association goes on to say that under Bill C-19, applicants will not even have to be regulated financial institutions in their home jurisdiction. Government policy will be that any institutions which are, "primarily engaged in the business of providing financial services" will qualify it to apply for a Schedule II bank licence. Also from the CBA, "There is no reference to indicate to bank regulation or indeed a requirement that the applicant be a regulated financial institution of any kind."
They go on, Mr. Speaker, and this is perhaps the most damaging comment from the CBA with respect to this bill, to say: "Last March, well before the demise of BCCI, we advised the finance committee that in our view the entry rules for Schedule II banks proposed in Bill C-19 do not represent sound public policy."
The president of the CBA went on to say: "In my view these recommendations for change take on new urgency in light of the BCCI failure."
What we have here, Mr. Speaker, is something extraordinary. We have an international conspiracy involved in BCCI which even the Canadian Bankers' Association, of which BCCI was a member, concludes leads to without doubt the recognition that the regulatory authority that we have established for foreign banks in this country is not sound public policy. Even the bankers say it is not sound public policy. How the government of this country can expect people in Canada to accept a piece of legislation like this, given the very sad experience of the depositors in the BCCI in Canada, and given the very harsh judgment of the Canadian bankers themselves with respect to this regulation of foreign banks, frankly, is beyond me.
BCCI is an international scandal. Ultimately the case of BCCI in Canada will be seen as a regulatory scandal. I think that this bill coming before us like this, not closing the loopholes on banks like BCCI in the future, is as much of a scandal to this House.
I therefore hope very much that responsible members of this House will recognize the gaps in this legislation, recognize that foreign banks are being given far too much of a free hand, recognize the dangers which the BCCI case so clearly demonstrates. Therefore, we will reject this legislation that is in front of us. I hope very much that not just those of us in the New Democratic
October 2, 1991

Party, but those throughout the entire House will see that we do not need more examples of BCCI and the loss of depositors' money in the future. We will reject these pieces of legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to stand in the House today to address these various pieces of legislation that deal with banks, co-operatives, credit associations, trust and insurance companies.
After having done considerable research and talked to people who are quite knowledgeable about this type of initiative, it seems to me that this package of legislation is a reasonable effort. It is a small step into the future, to make us more competitive, to bring about some greater degree of rationality to banks, trust companies, insurance companies and others. Hopefully it will permit additional flexibility in terms of the services offered to Canadians by banks, trust companies and insurance companies.
The major intent of this legislation is to ascertain that there is a similar range of services available to customers from those various institutions so that it is more competitive and hopefully the consumer will profit from that.
Insurance companies will now be able to own banks and trust companies and banks own insurance and trust companies. Banks will now be able to get into financial leasing and information processing companies. Hopefully that will bring about greater competition that will profit all Canadians.
I note, as well, that insurance companies will be able to lend money. Knowing the price that we have to pay today with high interest rates, it will permit those rates to drop and all Canadian consumers will profit.
When one looks at this legislation which covers hundreds of pages, actually hundreds of sections, one wonders what it is that one must do as a member of Parliament to attempt to ensure that Canadians are protected.
Government Orders
One of the questions that I want to raise is the following. What will government do with banks, trust and insurance companies to inform the Canadian public regarding what is happening? To ensure that when this bill becomes law that they understand the advantages, the disadvantages and the difficulties?

You no doubt know that it is extremely complicated. Even after speaking to many people and reading and considering this information, I admit that there are technicalities which are very hard to understand.
So I earnestly hope that the government will make a serious effort with these institutions to inform the general public.

My party supports this legislation in principle. However, we have a number of concerns, which will be raised in committee. I have heard a number of issues raised today by both opposition parties. The place to correct those is in committee. I would hope, as well, that the committee will be such that it will permit us to raise those issues and permit members to come to grips with them and bring about solutions so that in the end, when we have finished the process, we do have as fine a package as we can have.
A number of colleagues have noted that it is really high time that we come to grips with those kinds of issues, because it has been some 50 years or so since this legislation has been updated, but they have not said it in a negative kind of way.
It makes it increasingly difficult for us to compete in Canada. It makes it that much more difficult as well to compete on the international level. It is high time that we came to grips with this, because it will improve our competitiveness. It will I hope protect the depositors.
I cannot help but note that if this legislation had been in place there are a number of Canadians who would not have suffered the financial losses they have. I am referring, of course, to the failure of certain banks and trust companies. They would be better off today.

Because they would have been better protected, I hope. And frankly, if we could have proceeded sooner, hundreds, maybe thousands, of Canadians would have benefited from it.

I note one change which I am pleased with; one-third of the board of directors must not be affiliated with the company. I think that is a positive move.
I notice as well procedures for conflicts of interest. For example, an audit committee will be established which will deal with the auditor's report and any particular difficulties that emanate from that report. There will be a conduct review committee which will prevent selfdealing, where a director may have influence which could benefit him or her. It will prevent that kind of unacceptable practice.
Most important, however, is the consumer's complaint section. This section, I might add, is as a result of the Liberal amendment, and I am very pleased with that, will permit consumers to raise questions concerning service charges on accounts. A farmer, if he or she faces foreclosure, can go to the consumer complaints office and in fact to the superintendent if necessary.
There will also be an annual report where there will be a section on complaints, where those complaints will be described briefly and where it will be noted the kinds of successes that have been had in resolving those kinds of complaints.

I think that is progress. Mind you, some problems
remain. It is not perfect, but I think it is progress, especially if it can be further improved in committee.

The whole question of ownership, the percentage of a company that one can own according to the current legislation and what will happen with the new legislation is something that we have to look at very veiy carefully. Are the percentages correct? Are they too limited? Are they too generous? What are the implications of those changes? What about the current percentages? If my memory serves me correctly, you have to own at least 51 per cent or no more than 10 per cent of another institution. Will that prevent joint ventures, which is a very common way of acquiring another institution?
As well, you will note that the banks cannot go further into the insurance market. While there are some positives there, we have to ask ourselves is that best for Canadians? Is this good for Canadians? Is it better for Canadians?
We have to realize that banks are powerful institutions and if they were to proceed in that area, I understand that they could in fact destabilize the insurance industry. There could be tied selling, that is you do not get a mortgage unless, or you get a mortgage if, and that could be a dangerous practice. They could, in fact, implement very low prices for certain services and they could then have a monopoly and then control that. That would be bad for Canadians. So there are pluses and minuses on both sides of those particular issues.
When we talk about the life annuity market, we have to be veiy careful because while it is a life insurance company only now, as Canadians grow older, as they convert various plans into life annuities, as they must under certain circumstances, would it be wise to have banks involved so that we as aging Canadians can get better deals?
The whole notion of being involved or not involved in leasing is another question that needs to be looked at very, very carefully.
I want to address the question of foreign banks in Canada. The bank must be a bank in its home country before it can qualify according to the current legislation, the legislation before us. Why was American Express admitted?
October 2, 1991

AMEX is not a bank. Why was it let in? Some people suggest that because it supported the government significantly with respect to the Canada-U.S. trade agreement that it might have got preferential treatment. Whether it did or not is not the major issue. The issue is: What will happen to other companies that are of a very similar nature? Will they be asking to get in? If so, will they be denied? Do we want non-banks?
There are large financial institutions in the United States and in other places that could in fact be trying to get into the Canadian financial market. The fundamental question is do we want that?
Another issue is: Should the Minister of Finance be able to decide who qualifies as a foreign bank in order to get into Canada's financial market? I cannot help but note that because of the GATT negotiations, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade with other countries, that they may see a precedent that they may want to take advantage of and that may open up a whole new avenue to other financial institutions wanting to get into Canada.
Perhaps a final point before I sum up very quickly. There is still a duplication of federal and provincial rules, regulations, legislation and what have you between the trust companies and banks. I think this needs to be looked at because this kind of duplication obviously does not lead to greater efficiency.

Mr. Speaker, I will close by saying again that in principle we support the bill before us today. Nevertheless, we wish to improve it when it is considered in committee. I think it is a step forward.

I would hope that out of this, we would get the following: First, more protection for the consumer; better deals for the consumer in terms of those services that are required and I would hope, as well, that we can in fact become more competitive in the positive sense. That is, we as Canadians can get better protection, more services and still be competitive at the international level.

Mr. Speaker,
I too would like to join in with some of my colleagues, especially those on this side of the House in this party who have spoken so eloquently on some of the pitfalls in the legislation even though as a party in principle we are supporting it at second reading so that we can get it before a committee.
You have seen some of the pitfalls of this legislation. It is legislation that is designed, as my colleague from Dartmouth indicated earlier, specifically to set new financial infrastructure for a new economic order in this country.
In establishing that new financial infrastructure, we have got to maintain first and foremost very well in perspective the people for whom it is designed. It is designed not only for depositors as members of the NDP have said, but also for the borrowers, the consumers, the small businessman, the individual who is under attack today as a result of government policies and mismanagement of the highest order never before seen in this country.
I guess what I am saying is what we should be addressing is not only the over-all financial infrastructure but the scope of its dimensions. Where should it be going? What should it be addressing? If nothing else, it should be addressing the crux of many problems.
Many small businesses throughout Canada, in particular in my home province of Ontario and more specifically in the city of Toronto, are prone to say that banks and other lenders in times that are good, in times of prosperity, are the first ones to offer moneys and to say: "Let's be partners. Invest. Expand."
The moment that things fall apart, banks are the first ones to pull back and to leave the small businessman, the investor, the entrepreneur who is short on cash flow with a bank that demands its note, and demands it yesterday.
What has happened is that we have seen throughout all of Canada an increase in bankruptcies of an obscene order. They are of obscene order. We have never seen such bankruptcies at that rate ever in Canada.
I noticed today that the Minister of Finance, the Minister for International Trade and the Minister for Privatization all stood before us in this House and said:

"Oh yes, but there is a steadying trend, in fact, we do not have as many bankruptcies this last month as we have had in the past several months".
There are not that many more businesses available to go bankrupt. What is happening as well is that all of us as Canadian taxpayers are being turned into financiers in short order. What happens is that the moment there is a bankruptcy declared, Revenue Canada needs to get its share. There are some moneys that have not been paid that are owing to Revenue Canada, to the Minister of Revenue, and what happens is that the taxpayer ends up on the short end of a deal as well. We end up paying twice: first, for having lost our businesses and jobs available through it, and second, because our taxes have not been paid.
We have to take a look at what these acts are going to do by way of establishing incentives for our entrepreneurs. Small businessmen, entrepreneurs of all sizes need access to capital. They need to establish working capital as they anticipate growing cash flow.
I do not know whether this series of legislation is going to address that, but one of the things the government must address is the fact that these acts cannot operate in a vacuum. They have to establish appropriate economic policies that allow the Canadian entrepreneur to have access to capital on an equal basis, no matter in what province he or she chooses to operate.
For example, I have a company, the Hercules Food Equipment, Limited, in Toronto, Ontario, in my own city which bemoans the fact that just over the course of the year, it has lost over 50 per cent of all fabricators of food equipment in the stainless steel industry. Over 50 per cent, Mr. Speaker. It points out the fact that unfortunately, thanks to government policies, not only in encouraging the transmigration of some of these industries over into the southern part of our borders in the northeastern United States, but that government policies seem to misdirected and pitting one province against another, and unfairly pitting one Canadian against another. They faxed me a list of 28 public projects that the stainless steel producing industry for food processing has been unable to secure in the southern Ontario area, but have gone to another area, to companies that locate in Quebec.
There is nothing wrong with that because Canadians are Canadians no matter where they go, but the fact of the matter is that what we have is an economic policy that encourages movement southward. Why do I say it encourages movement southward. When we signed that free trade agreement, we did not get the security we needed to ensure that the playing field would be level. We have New York state, Ohio and other Great Lakes states that are providing our manufacturers with kinds of tax incentives on capital equipment, on property, on subsidies to employees, and as well on the general operations that we cannot afford here in Canada.
Our federal government has not addressed that at all. In fact, not only has it not addressed that, but we see Canadian companies going south in droves. Just last year, 83 Canadian companies set up shop in the Buffalo area alone. Buffalo used to be a joke in southern Ontario. It is now a nemesis for all of us.
My colleague from Broadview-Greenwood said there is a waiting list of Canadian companies that number in the thousands to locate in Buffalo. Last year my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood will know that Canadian companies invested $263 million in Buffalo alone, $263 million at a time when all of our Canadian manufacturers, Canadian employees or prospective employees are looking for that kind of cash flow.
To what is that due? Nothing else other than a Canadian federal government that is unwilling to seize the responsibility that lies on its shoulders. It is a responsibility that says that what we have to do is have an overall global strategy that involves reforming all of our financial institutions, an industrial strategy that ensures that government incentives are at least equal to those that are provided south of our border, or at least are equitable from province to province so that we do not have competing interests from Quebec or from Ontario, but rather that we be co-operative and complementary.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin this afternoon by thanking the member for Nickel Belt. He is our critic and he keeps our caucus informed on the many changes that are proposed in these four bills. The reason I want to thank him this afternoon is that this morning I was cursing him because as I walked into my office, yet again there was another thick file from our critic on these four bills. I was trying to read through it and pick up what had been done in committee and what was proposed in each particular piece of legislation, the comments, the critiques that have been put forward, and it struck me as I went through the material that I have at least access to this information. Most of us, as Canadians, do not.
In a technical sense I suppose you could say these are not secret documents. They are public documents. They are matters which are available to the public, but then again is it a reasonable assumption that the public can go through all these little differences that are being proposed in these four bills, understand, for example, all the fine nuances between a bank not being able to sell insurance but being able to set up an insurance company. What is the difference?
That, I think, is one of the hallmarks of the Canadian financial institutions. Canadians have always assumed that if it looks like a bank, smells like a bank, and when they go in there they are made line up, then it must be a bank. When you read the fine print you find out it is not a bank. It is something else.
Canadians have had a summer where there has been a healthy amount of newspaper copy written about something that was called a bank but really was not a bank. It did not have proper credentials in its own country but was set up and operating here as a bank. Even embassies were using this bank, but that bank somehow had some wrong connections. There was enough juiciness around that one that I suppose Canadians aware that maybe not all banks are the same, maybe not all lending institutions are the same. Most of us, I am sure, when we started our working lives were ever so grateful when the manager at the local bank said: "Yes, we are going to give you that loan for a new car". We were just so grateful that we

Government Orders
were such good credit risks that a bank would lend us money that we forgot to read the fine print.
Later on in life we found out why it is that lending institutions are just overjoyed to give you a really long-term mortgage on a house. Some time in your life you probably sat down and figured out just exactly how much of this money that you pay each month to a lending institution pays off the principal of the debt and how much of it goes into juice to the lending institution. The first time you do that most Canadians are absolutely shocked that this nice, warm, friendly, trusting person who arranged all of these financial transactions for you that made you feel so good, so much a part of the Canadian economy, had just ripped you for about 20 years of your life.
After a while you kind of begin to understand: Let us all read the fine print here, let us just try to figure out who is doing whom a favour.
I must say that in dealing with lending institutions these days I find, just as a general simplification, there seems to be a little more aura of laying out the facts before you. I recall when somebody sold me my first insurance policy. As a matter of fact this one was supposed to get my kids through university. That is a noble thing. I thought that was a great idea: "Why do we not invest in our children's future? This is wonderful. Are these companies not great to be putting out this kind of a policy that will help me when my child is 18 years of age? I do not have to worry about a college education. The money is in the bank".
It is a good thing I did not quite follow all of that line because I subsequently found out that if I had taken that money to a piggy bank I would have been just about as well off as buying that life insurance policy. Nobody bothered to explain that to me at the time, and the person who sold me the policy was not an evil person. They did not catch me in the backyard with a billy club. They came in and sat down at my kitchen table and explained: "Isn't this a wonderful thing to do?" Well of course it is. Investing in your children's future is what all of us want to do. That is part of my concern about these bills.
Most Canadians have an assumption in terms of the great Canadian tradition that the government is going to be around, that there will be an agency to regulate and it will be an outside agency. It will not be self-regulation. Most Canadians understand that a financial institution is
in business to make money. That is what they are going to do as best they can, following the laws of the land to the letter and sometimes a little past the letter and sometimes a little to the left of the letter and sometimes a little right of the letter. The purpose of the exercise is clearly stated: to make money as legally as they can with the help of a whole lot of really good lawyers, a lot of accountants, a lot of smart tax people, and some friends on the government side.
That is my concern in a nutshell about what is happening here. It is not that on the surface of it, it looks like a lot of evil deeds. But when one gets into the detail of what is being proposed here, that age old assumption that Canadians have had that their financial institutions are well and thoroughly regulated by an independent party is out the window. There were those of us who got a little pious over things like the savings and loans scandals in the United States. We were concerned that here were lending institutions that started out in the United States of America a long time ago with a very simply idea of offering a little diversity for the financing of houses. They offered a little opportunity for ordinary people to get mortgage money in a way that had not been done previously. That really good idea, that gem of a thought somehow wound up in the hands of people who were so greedy that it did not bother them that they were mortgaging properties to values that were astronomical. Commercial investment opportunities that were worth $50 million wound up being mortgaged to the tune of a $200 million.
How did that happen? That happened very simply because there was not in place a regulatory agency independent of those handling the money. That is part of my concern with what is being proposed here. I think all of us rightfully made the assumption that Canadian financial institutions were somehow distinctively Canadian, regulated by an independent agency, would do us no wrong, were safe things and all that stuff about our deposits being insured to a certain extent. People do not read those last few words in that line: to a certain extent, to a maximum, in some circumstances. People had better learn to read that.
Most of us who have been in public life for a while have had someone come into our offices-and this is the irony, especially for a New Democrat-who was certainly not a political ally but told us about a friend of theirs who
October 2, 1991

got them into an investment with a particular kind of company. Since this was the great free enterprise system at work and since their friend had initiated all of the proceeding-had got them into it, took all their life savings and put them into this institution-they somehow assumed that in Canada this could not go wrong.
The tragedy of course is that it has gone wrong. Many times many of us have sat in our constituency offices with someone who was not a political ally crying because the system that they purported to be very much theirs had ruined their lives. People are beginning now to understand that this is a pretty complicated business.
The federal government regulates, writes legislation in this regard. The provincial governments write legislation in similar matters. We are now going into a constitutional proposal that is going to mix that rather nicely and maybe have an economic council that has an influence and an impact on all that.
Here is the problem. When governments at all levels say "what shall we do", they do not drag in the consumers by the thousands. That is perhaps impractical. What they do is they turn to people working in the industry and they say: "What changes shall we make that would make the industry more competitive"-read that to mean makes more money-"or more efficient?" Read that to mean pays out less money.
We must understand what is going on here. This is pretty basic stuff. These are all legitimate questions to be asking, but one does not always ask those who are in the business to be one's sole advisors on what a government should be, on what things a government should do, on what kind of regulations a government should put in place, on what kind of laws a government should write. That is the flaw that I find in the legislation that is before this evening.
I know that most Canadians probably are not listening to this debate. Most of them will probably never read these bills. Most of them may not be followers of Business Week and all of the financial critiques that have been put together on these four bills. Canadians had better become aware that there is a major change under way in those things that are loosely called financial institutions and most of us would call banks. I pray that they do not become aware of those changes in my

constituency office when something awful has happened to them, no matter who they might be.
That is precisely the danger in what is being proposed here this afternoon. It requires an immense amount of study, an immense amount of research, and the players are dictating the rules. That is never a good way to proceed.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to say a few words on this bill before we get on to the next one.
We are in a new age and certainly there are new requirements in the banking business in this country if we are going to be competitive. If we do not give the small business community of this nation a better banking policy, it is not going to continue to be the biggest employer in Canada and the economy of this nation is going to suffer still more.
What small businesses need today more than anything else is working capital. Without that they cannot progress. Without that they cannot keep their employees. Without that they cannot continue to build and maintain their present facilities so that they are ready to meet the new economy when the recession is over.
I had a meeting during the course of the last year with several business people from the resource based industries. The local bank was after them the moment that the 15 per cent export tax went on softwood lumber. The bank sent a man into a certain branch and he continued to phone those business people who had loans there and demanded the money. It was totally an unfair situation.
What was going on south of the border at that time? The American banks and trust companies saw that 15 per cent tax on softwood lumber as a great ploy for them to move in, and they started loaning money and offering money to their resource based industries. They improved their sawmilling capacity, their planing mills and their lumber industry in general. They had better equipment, did a better job. As a result they took the Canadian market away from Canadian business people in Canada.
They even sold lumber back into Canada, cheaper than we could sell it to the United States. Those northern industries in the U.S. took over markets in the United States as far south as Tennessee from business people in Canada. That is not fairness.

October 2, 1991
Government Orders
Yet a Canadian bank moved in on those very people, the sawmill industry. It had worked with them for decades and never had a problem. That is how loyal the banking system of this nation is to small business in this country.
It is time that this Parliament of Canada starts passing banking bills. I have been in this House for some time and I cannot remember a banking bill ever being passed in this House in favour of the consumer or the business people of the country. We have a sound banking system, but it is sound because the people out there are being crucified as soon as the economy begins a downturn.
When the economy is good everybody wants to lend money to the business community, to consumers; banks have all kinds of money to give out. As soon as the economy turns bad they turn on those customers.
Banks sometimes even encourage them to borrow. Banks encouraged farmers to borrow several years ago and got many of them into trouble. Today we have a farm crisis in this country and the banks do not even want to look at it.
Someone mentioned bankruptcies in this country. It is no wonder that we have bankruptcies with the challenges that small business people and others are facing out there. This Parliament of Canada owes it to those people, who are the biggest employers in this country, to bring in some banking legislation to give them some protection in difficult times such as now.
A lot has been said in this House in the last number of months about the downturn of the economy and the slow economy in places like Montreal and Toronto. People find that astounding because these two urban centres of Canada are usually very much on the upswing. There is a big reason why those two major cities in Canada are having trouble and it has never really been talked about. The economy of the regions of this country is in difficult straits. Because those two major urban centres do not have the healthy economies of the regions of the country to draw on ,they are suffering a downturn in their own economies.
As long as we have banking legislation in this country which allows banks to impose their authority, their demands on the business community of this country, all we are doing is promoting a greater and greater recession the moment there is a downturn in the economy.
I was appalled at the treatment a group of forest industries in my riding received from their local bank. The banker they dealt with had no mercy.
It is rather amusing. I phoned the head office of the bank and it was turned over to its regional officer working out of Ottawa. He came in as a trouble-shooter. That is exactly what he was. Two days before we had that meeting with the rep from that bank and with the sawmilling people in the area, the local banker disappeared from the scene. He was hauled out because he had created bad relations and bad spirit in the surrounding community for the bank.
I am simply going to leave this thought with the House, and it certainly should be discussed when this bill is in committee.
We should be coming up with some legislation in this House that is going to protect the business community of this country, the small businessman and those people who employ the largest number of people coast to coast to coast in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I guess I would like to add my voice from the far west coast in this debate on the Canadian banking system and the proposals that we have before us to change the financial institutions in Canada, to open them up and to take over each other's business.
I guess I am a little concerned about this legislation as well. I do hope that these bills form the basis of a discussion that can take place when it is referred to committee across Canada. I think the parliamentarians, especially on the government side, will find out that in drafting this legislation they have been listening to a very narrow range of opinion in this country. If they open the debate within the committee that handles this legislation, they are going to get a very different message from people across the country as to how they would like their financial institutions to act and how they would like financial institutions to serve the people of this country.
Canadian banks have traditionally been among the most powerful financial institutions on the globe. It is strange that in a country with a population of 20 million to 30 million we have banks that rank among the most powerful banks on earth in terms of the assets they
October 2, 1991

control and the power they exert in business around the world.
It is hard to explain when you consider the size of our population and the actual deposit base that they have to work from. One of the reasons for that and one of the reasons for the power of the banking system in this country is that they have been able to exert a great deal of power and control over this very institution in which we stand.
They donate to the two main political parties in this country, and they influence how those political parties deal with banking legislation. They have close contacts and interlocking contacts with the corporate sector in this country. They influence the business of this country to a great extent through those interlocking contacts.
They have the power to influence banking policy and it is clear that that influence has been exerted in this legislation. It is clear to see that the bankers, the insurance companies, the trust company executives, and the financial institutions have had a great deal to say about the legislation that is before us now.
The American Express example that our friend from the Liberal Party mentioned was probably an exception that proved the rule. This is one that the Canadian Banking Association was opposed to, but it is one of the very few times when it attempted to influence the government. It has not been successful in influencing it in exactly the way it wanted.
In fact, what the member suggested is precisely what happened. When the Prime Minister was concerned that his party was going to lose the last election, that his Conservatives would end up out of government and the free trade policy on which they had hung their hat was going to be defeated by Canadians, he called upon one of his cronies in the American Express system from the United States and that person recruited a great deal of funding and a great deal of support both in Canada and in the United States.
They advertised in the major media across the country and began to turn the tide in the last election in favour of the Conservatives, and the Prime Minister's cronies in the United States got their reward: they got the Conservative government re-elected and they got their free trade policy.
Government Orders
American Express also got its reward. On the eve of the election it got a charter to set up a bank in Canada, even though it is not a banking corporation in the country in which it originates, the United States.
That is a way in which banking policy can be influenced in this country, by applying political influence on behalf of the government in power. There is no question that the banks do that.
The banks' influence on government has also come in other ways and in other fields. For example, I have been in banks all across this country and talked to trade unionists about their success in organizing chartered banks. Across this country the number of banks which are organized and have unionized staff can probably be counted on the fingers of both hands.
That is because banks have been able to impose their influence on provincial and federal governments to ensure that it is extremely difficult to organize the workers in chartered banks so that they cannot form unions, cannot organize and bargain collectively, and cannot set up grievance procedures in order to protect themselves and secure their jobs.
Banks are the most patriarchal employers in this country. They are the most medieval in terms of the standards they impose on their employees. In general, bank managers are male, upper middle class, elderly, with a particular point of view about the country and its economy. They tend to appoint as their staff members people who have the same characteristics and the same beliefs.
For example, we have federal employment equity legislation in this country governing companies that operate within the federal jurisdiction, among which are the chartered banks. Yet for some reason the current government refuses to put teeth in that employment equity legislation. That would require the corporations operating within their jurisdiction to actually bring about employment equity within their organizations.
The banks have been among the worst in terms of hiring women and promoting women to management positions. They have been among the worst in terms of hiring aboriginal people. In appointing aboriginal people to management positions, banks have been among the worst. In incorporating the handicapped and the dis-

October 2, 1991
Government Orders
abled, banks have been among the worst. That is because they have been able to influence and persuade government because of their power over government to leave the teeth out of the employment equity legislation.
The same thing applies to pay equity legislation. Women who are employed in the chartered banks tend to be employed in jobs that are extremely low paying relative to the jobs occupied by men in the chartered bank system. Again this is an area that is within the federal jurisdiction. Yet there is absolutely no legislation to protect those women or to incorporate pay equity in the chartered banks and financial institutions that come under the jurisdiction of the federal government.
All of these things have been a result of the banks' ability to exert power over the federal government. Things have been absolutely the opposite of the way they should be. Instead of being the regulated, banks are actually the regulators which are regulating the federal government. It is not the other way around.
I do not think, as my colleague suggested, that customers of chartered banks are going to be secure until they feel secure that the federal government is actually regulating the chartered banks and imposing tough regulations with teeth.
I would like to close by talking about income tax legislation. In the average year the bank tellers working on the floors of those chartered banks pay more income tax to this Parliament than the banks do themselves, despite the horrendous profits those banks are making. The burden of taxation in this country has been totally distorted and totally turned on its head.
It is to be expected that in a country like this there would be no representation without taxation. Yet the banks have more representation in this country, despite the fact they pay no tax, than the tellers who work in those banks without the protection of labour laws, without the protection of trade unions, without the protection of employment equity legislation, without the protection of pay equity legislation. Even though they pay more tax to support the government of this country, they appear to have no representation in the drafting of legislation with respect to financial institutions.
I support my colleague who is voting against this legislation. I hope that when it goes into committee that the discussion will be wide ranging and that we will not listen to that narrow range of people who appear to have had influence in drafting this legislation. I hope that we will listen to all of the Canadian people in terms of the concerns that they have about their banks and institutions, and I hope that having heard those concerns the government will be prepared to pull and redraft this legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a plethora of information here and I am going to have to put it in a brief form.
When I spoke last I was saying that in Canada we go to great lengths to be positive when we are building something. We have some tremendous achievements in this country, but once we achieve them we seem to want to tear them apart. This bill that is before us, Bill C-204,
Private Members' Business
is designed to phase out the generation of electricity by nuclear power in Canada.
I am unreservedly and totally opposed to this bill, because I think it is terrible. In the 1950s Canada produced an Arrow aircraft which was considered to be the best in the world. We had a change of government and by 1960 the plane had been cancelled. It would still have been a good plane today and Canada lost that technology.
It is unfair in this debate for people to talk about nuclear weapons in the same tone that they use when they talk about nuclear energy. That is not fair. It is dishonest debating.
Sometimes we have to go outside our own country in order to find people who are proud of our achievements. For example, when the Challenger space shuttle needed repairs, where did they go? They went to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, which had been known for good production and technology over the years. They were known for their Candu reactor, which has never had an accident and was equipped with many safety features, even for human error. That has never come out.
The United States came to Canada, to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. Atomic Energy of Canada made the O-ring for the Challenger space shuttle and it has been successful ever since. Again we had to go outside our country to be recognized.
Other people compare Chernobyl and the Russian reactor to the Candu reactor. That is absolutely dishonest politics. There is no comparison between the two. The Russians built their systems without any safety features built into them and they got the problem they deserved. Here in Canada the reason why our Candu reactors are so expensive is that we have built safety devices into them and we have never had an accident.
We sometimes think that the only thing you get radiation from around here is the nuclear industry. I am reminded of the story-and it is not just a story; it is a fact of life-where daughter number one, for example, wanted to work in Toronto at the top of the CN tower for the summer or go to the Darlington nuclear plant. Experts will tell you that she would get a greater radiation dose at the top of the CN tower in Toronto than she would have had at the Darlington nuclear plant

Private Members' Business
because of the safety features built into Darlington. Of course in nature, the higher you go in space the more radiation you get. That is why stewardesses who are pregnant are not allowed to go on long flights at certain times during their pregnancy. It is a safety measure. That is nature.
There are many countries in this world that have taken Canada's lead. They do not have the same kind of reactor we have. Here is an example. In France, 74.5 per cent of France's electrical power is generated by nuclear power. In Belgium, 60.1 per cent; the Republic of Korea, 49.1 per cent; in Sweden, 45.9 per cent. Sweden is a country that decided it might phase out the nuclear option too and it is already reconsidering that option.
If Canada is going to get its debt under control then it needs to have a buoyant economy creating wealth. It is not a given right that Canada's traditional wealth creating industries, that is our resources, will continue to perform as they have in the past. Nor is it true that our manufacturing and agricultural industries can compete internationally. The assets we have which can give us a competitive edge are the abundant energy resources of oil, natural gas, coal, hydro, nuclear and biomass, to name a few.
I want to say here that as an educator I am absolutely astounded at the uninformed opinion that is being projected by those who speak negatively about nuclear energy for peaceful purposes. Scare tactics are being used and it is totally unfair to the integrity of this debate in Canada. Christopher Columbus was warned by a similar mentality that if he travelled too far out to sea he would fall off the end of the world. If such were the case, the Ontario voters would probably be sending the NDP Government of Ontario on a long voyage tomorrow morning.
In summing up, I want to say that wise decisions will promote success; poor ones will guarantee failure. If this bill ever sees the light of day in legislation, then we have failed and the nation has failed.
In Ontario alone, which is the heartland of industry in all of Canada, 53 per cent of hydroelectric power will be produced by nuclear power when Darlington comes on stream. We are seeing an attack on our capacity to produce jobs and on industrial growth down the road in Canadian history. The greatest asset we have in this nation ig cheap energy. With all the other things we have
to compete with in this world tomorrow and the next day after, we are going to need a long-term solid base for industry in this country. That solid base is going to be cheap energy.
In closing, I want to say that the nuclear generation of power is safe in that it does not spew gasses out into the environment. It is one of the safest things going.

maintopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 7.03 p.m.
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to carry on with the second reading debate of Bill C-204, a bill introduced by my colleague from Winnipeg Transcona.
I invite our viewers tonight to read his speech of June 11 of this year given with the introduction of this bill. It does give a comprehensive overview of the entire issue.
As I am limited in time I will focus only on two aspects of the nuclear phase out: the economic aspect and the environmental. We are often told that the two should be linked. It is those two aspects I have chosen to focus my comments on.
I am going to start with the economic argument because increasingly this government seems to be instituting a philosophy of economic determinism, that is economics determines its policy. I invite people to understand that the economics of the nuclear industry is bad economics.
Federal tax dollars have funded the development of nuclear technology. It has been estimated in a study published by the Economic Council of Canada that $19 billion-that is billion with a b in 1990 dollars-was given in federal subsidies, including grants for research and development, loan guarantees and bailouts for prototype reactors and heavy water plants. "It is doubtful", the Economic Council of Canada states in this study, "that these costs will never be recovered".
If we are talking about economic determinism this is bad economics. We are never going to get our money back for the investment we make.
The Canadian nuclear industry does rely on government subsidies to stay alive. Atomic Energy of Canada Limited continues to receive over $200 million each year from Canadian taxpayers. Mr. Speaker, you and I and all those other people out there are funding the nuclear industry whether we like it or not.
This is in contravention of what I think most Canadians want. The previous government in 1979, under the then Prime Minister, the current Minister responsible
October 2, 1991

for Constitutional Affairs, promised a public inquiry into the nuclear industry. Just prior to the 1984 election there was a promise of a public inquiry into the nuclear industry. Again, in 1989 the then Minister of the Environment, who is now currently the head of the Bloc Quebecois, and the current Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources promised a public review of nuclear power. We have not yet had it.
This bill, Bill C-204, is our chance to have a public debate at long last on the nuclear industry. We also have to know what the economic costs are. In terms of capital costs nuclear plants are extremely expensive to build. The cost of the Darlington nuclear station is estimated at about $2.5 billion. Hydro's newest estimate for Darlington is about $12.8 billion. It is not just the cost in dollars that we have to talk about, it is the environmental cost. That is what I want to talk about now, and particularly the issue of high level nuclear waste.
Inside every nuclear reactor, hundreds of radioactive substances are created, substances that did not exist before nuclear technology was developed. They are among the most toxic materials known to science. No one knows how to dispose of them.
Spent nuclear fuel is so radioactive that it can never be handled by human hands. It must be handled by robotic equipment. Spent nuclear fuel will remain unapproachable for several centuries and extremely toxic for hundreds of thousands of years.
Nuclear wastes are also deadly in another way. They contain the raw material for nuclear weapons. Plutonium is the key ingredient in nuclear bombs. Through a process of reprocessing plutonium can be separated from spent fuel. The nuclear industry supports reprocessing because plutonium can also be used to fuel reactors.
Although the Canadian government has not approved commercial scale reprocessing AECL, funded by our tax dollars, has promoted it and practised it on a small scale.
Over 17,000 tonnes of used nuclear fuel bundles are now being stored at reactor sites in Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick. Canada is being put forward as a nuclear waste disposal site for the world. Both Japan and
Private Members' Business
the United States have helped finance AECUs disposal research.
A former energy minister wrote in 1984 that disposing of nuclear wastes from other countries could offer considerable commercial benefits. I want a public debate on this issue because the Canadian taxpayers do not know what their tax dollars are being used for. If they knew there would be an outcry of monumental proportions.
AECL has spent over 10 years attempting to prove that deep disposal in a geologic repository is the answer to high level nuclear waste. AECL has spent hundreds of millions of dollars attempting to confirm a single solution, a deep geological repository for nuclear waste.
There is a more fundamental problem with Canada's nuclear waste disposal program. It has been conceived and implemented by individuals and institutions committed to the preservation of the nuclear industry. We only hear one side of the issue. AECL's mandate is to promote the use of nuclear power in Canada and abroad. Its interests would not be served by demonstrating the weakness of the concept of deep geological disposal or by admitting that not enough is known to reach a scientific verdict.
This issue has been before this House many times. A 1988 report of the federal Standing Committee on Environment and Forestry entitled The Eleventh Hour, a very aptly named report, recommended unanimously that a moratorium on the construction of nuclear power plants in Canada should be imposed until the people of Canada have agreed on an acceptable solution to the problem of the disposal of high level radioactive waste. That has not yet occurred.
This is what we have before us now. If this bill passes second reading it will then go to committee, which will have the ability to call witnesses, both experts and representatives of organizations. The nuclear industry will be there. We are not afraid to debate them. We encourage the debate. We encourage the forum so that Canadian taxpayers can know what their tax dollars are being used for.
I challenge the government and the Liberal members opposite because the New Democratic Party is the only party with a nuclear phase-out policy.

Private Members' Business
As a member of the Commons committee of the environment that participated in an 18 month study of global climate change and made a report in March of this year entitled "Out of Balance: The Risk of Irreversible Climate Change", it has been demonstrated in that report that this nuclear power is uneconomic, immoral and a waste of the taxpayers' dollars. Alternative energy is the way to go.
I encourage the viewers tonight to read the comments of my colleague from Winnipeg Transcona and I challenge the government and the Liberals to pass this bill at second reading so we can call the government to account for the way they spend taxpayers' money.
