speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope we have Point Lepreau II before we are done and that is one of the reasons that I am pleased to speak about this.
I would, first of all, like to say how pleased I am to follow the previous speaker who was my colleague on the environment committee when we did the study on global warming which made reference to the use of nuclear power. I do not have the exact words at the end of that report, but they were words to the effect that nuclear power does have a place and does deserve further examination and did not draw any uneconomic conclusions at all.
Some of the NDP-introduced witnesses would have you believe that, but I am going to quote a witness here in a few minutes that makes the different point.
The proposed Bill C-204, as I understand it, will prevent the Atomic Energy Control Board from issuing any new licences related to almost all aspects of the nuclear industry in Canada for the next 50 years. It will, if passed, have serious effects on Canada's economy, its environment, the general health of its population and its standing in the international community.
The economic impact is expressed in terms of the fact that the nuclear industry in Canada presently provides well in excess of 30,000 jobs for Canadians. Their efforts serve through corporations and utilities to contribute $3.6 billion or more in economic activity to the Canadian economy each year and this contribution will obviously decline dramatically if the resolution contained in Bill C-204 is passed.
In terms of environmental impact, I would like to speak briefly, as I have in the environment committee in the past. Global warming in particular is a phenomenon that I think we all agree is caused by the emissions of carbon dioxide generally resulting from the burning of fossil fuels. The greatest threat in terms of the burning of fossil fuels in the foreseeable half century in the world will come from the development of huge coal resources in places like China and India.
The Canadian nuclear technology has the potential to supplant that coal production with a benign source of energy that will in fact make a very dramatic intrusion on the potential for global warming in the years ahead.
It seems to me that we have got to address the environmental issue, not from the fear of a nuclear accident. That is a fear that we all would have. I would like to elaborate for a few minutes about the fact that those fears perhaps are not as justified as they may seem. The real fear, in my view, in the world is global warming, in environmental terms and in terms of this debate. When it comes right down to confronting the probability of global warming, if we do not get the emissions of carbon dioxide under control, confronting that reality with the perceived risk even of a nuclear accident, I believe that the prospects for nuclear development and the Canadian record for safety and technological excellence far outweigh any of the risks that are involved.
I want to quote, almost verbatim, from an address from Dr. Robin Armstrong, the present president of the University of New Brunswick, previously the Dean of Science at the University of Toronto and one of Canada's top physicists. He says that the discussion of nuclear power reactors often generates more heat than light. The issues that are most often raised concerning nuclear power are three in number, the possibility of a catastrophic accident, the effect of radiation leakage on the population living in the vicinity and the ultimate disposal of the spent fuel.
In the more than 30 years, he says, that nuclear power reactors have been operating in North America, there has not been a single catastrophic accident. The most serious accident was at Three Mile Island. The containment design of the building there prevented any significant release of radiation.
October 2, 1991

In the case of Chernobyl in Ukraine as one of the hon. members has already mentioned, that accident, that design and the lack of precautions in its design and management were so profound as to not be comparable to the Canadian safety record and not represent really an example at all. The Russian example is really a red herring.
Over the past two decades, a vast quantity of research has been done to evaluate reactor safety. The risk to the public is defined as being very small, not zero but very, very small.
He quantifies these in the form of a risk assessment analysis. For an individual in this Chamber tonight, the probability of developing a fatal cancer as a result of a serious accident at the Lepreau 1 station which the hon. member has mentioned in New Brunswick is 2,000 times less than the probability of developing one as a result of exposure to the radiation from the radio elements naturally present in the environment.
That is what he means as "not significant". Therefore, if you accept the validity of that kind of risk assessment analysis, you can conclude that there really is no risk of a catastrophic accident from western style nuclear power reactor.
With respect to the issue of the disposal of high level wastes from nuclear reactors, these must be considered in relation to the relatively small amounts of waste material created by a nuclear power station. The methods for disposal are well known, and the principles of the technology have been the study of very intensive research.
The waste is placed in sealed corrosion resistant containers very deep within stable rock formations. Studies have shown that radioactive material moves extremely slowly through rock and in fact hundreds, indeed thousands of times slower than the groundwater through the same material.
Therefore, even if the containers were eventually breached, no significant amount of radiation would reach the surface. The fact is that after a time of only 500 years, the health hazard posed by the fission products created for one kilogram of the uranium waste is the same as the health hazard of radioactivity of the same amount of uranium occurring naturally in the earth's crust. The conclusion is that the waste disposal problem has been solved.
Private Members' Business
In the few minutes remaining, I want to draw another analogy and that is a policy analogy related to Sweden. It is interesting to observe that in 1980, a referendum in Sweden determined that a policy for the phasing out of nuclear power by the year 2010 should be declared, endorsed and implemented.
It was decided that starting in 1995, the first of the operating nuclear power plants should be taken out of service and decommissioned. It was only when they tried to establish what alternatives should be used to replace the 41 per cent of the country's electricity generation being produced by nuclear plants that the difficulties really became apparent to the decision makers.
The problem replacing the nuclear capacity was compounded by two other decisions taken by the Swedish government. One was not to increase the carbon dioxide produced by fossil fuels and the other was not to use any of Sweden's untapped rivers to produce hydropower.
Sweden also, of course, wanted to remain competitive in terms of its export industries to the world. Today, the government has abandoned that plan to phase out the first nuclear plant in 1995, and the industrial unions are reputed to have played a strong role in that decision.
It just goes to show that the resolution such as has been introduced here in Bill C-204 and the resolutions such as have been proposed by my colleagues in the NDP are not sustainable. The facts are that nuclear power does have a place. I hope eventually that it has a place in New Brunswick.
I must say that as a New Brunswicker, I am very distressed to see that our government has delayed its commitment to the AECL proposal. It looks as though the nuclear plant, the Candu III reactor that represented such a regional opportunity for the modular manufacturing of nuclear equipment for years and years to come may very well have gone to Saskatchewan, and I would be veiy interested in the position taken by the Saskatchewan NDP with respect to nuclear power now that it is in the midst of a major election campaign which the polls indicate it is intended to win.
I would not want to wish the people of Saskatchewan any bad luck. It would be enough bad luck if they got an NDP government, but it would be intensified bad luck if that NDP government made the decision to ultimately

October 2, 1991
Private Members' Business
discontinue the initiative the present Government of Saskatchewan has introduced.
Perhaps in the fullness of time the province of New Brunswick will yet be the beneficiary of NDP policy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-204. It is a private member's bill introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona in which he proposes to phase out nuclear energy in this country.
The hon. member of course does not live in the province of Ontario, which is something like 50 per cent to 60 per cent dependent on nuclear energy for our primary source of base power generation. It is interesting that parties talk about phasing out nuclear energy when they are in opposition. Certainly Mr. Peterson in Ontario talked vaguely about that when he was in the opposition; he was not going to complete the Darlington generating station. When he came to power and looked at today's realities, not only the economic realities but the environmental realities, suddenly he decided that he would complete the Darlington electrical generating stations.
It is interesting, after hearing from the NDP member from British Columbia, that Mr. Rae, the current premier of Ontario, had the same policy when he was in opposition. Now that he is premier of the province he is spending $2 billion or $3 billion to complete the two final phases of the Darlington electrical generating station, which involves some 900 megawatts for each one of those four stations. It is interesting that he is completing those stations.
The question is whether you have responsibility or not. This bill does not examine the responsible management of our resources, the realities facing the Ontario government or the ability of the Ontario hydroelectrical generating agency to provide electrical energy for the province of Ontario. It has placed before the people of
Ontario a plan for the next 25 years which proposes a number of alternatives.
The number one alternative is conservation. I do not think there is anybody in this House, in Canada, or any political party who believes that conservation is the best means of saving electrical energy, whether it is the retrofitting of our industry, a new design of light bulbs or whatever techniques are used.
That is the number one alternative put forward in the Ontario Hydro plan. It goes on to say that we must determine how much acid rain we want to create by using coal fired generating stations as our base station, how much we want to contribute to the greenhouse effect. It continues to say that if we reach a limit in that direction then the balance must be nuclear.

There are alternatives, such as small hydro sites, but hydro sites have an environmental cost as well. There is a whole generation generally classed in with conservation. For the Government of Canada to say "okay, Ontario, you may be 60 per cent dependent on nuclear energy, but we are stopping the licensing of any nuclear generating stations", surely that would be presumptuous and certainly not in keeping with a responsible way to develop the resource.
The argument is put forward by those who sponsored this bill that maybe we do not really want to do away with nuclear energy or phase it out; maybe we just want to have a public debate. I believe that the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources of the House of Commons did a major study back in 1987 and 1988. Its report was entitled Nuclear Energy: Unmasking the Mystery. It heard from dozens and dozens of witnesses.
The people from the NDP who sponsor this resolution tonight should read this report. It is a broad based report. It is not a fire and brimstone report. It talks about the advantages and disadvantages on all sides, but generally it comes down supporting the use of nuclear power as a source of electrical energy, as some of the most successful economies in the world are using. I speak especially of Japan and West Germany. Their main source of base power supply is nuclear energy.
We do not only have this document, which was a broad based study by a committee of this House. It is not as if the House of Commons is going to sit in Committee of

the Whole if this bill were to be passed. It will be returned to a committee, probably this committee. Someone can ask if parliamentary committees really do have the capacity to pay interveners and all that and how much time do members have to do a really thorough study?
That argument can be made. A study is taking place in the province of Ontario by a royal commission, a commission under the Environmental Assessment Act, dealing with both the needs and demand. It is an environmental study. It is not talking about abstracts. It is talking about the province of Ontario, which during the next 25 years has to replace 25 per cent of its electrical generating capacity. There are literally hundreds of interveners. There are some from my constituency and some from other areas on both sides of the issue of nuclear energy. It is sponsored by the Ontario government to put its best arguments forward on how we provide electrical energy for the province of Ontario.
Shall it be coal? Shall it be nuclear energy? Will it be small hydro sites? Will it be natural gas turbine fired engines? I mean all those things will be sorted out.
It will take about two years to do the demand study. How much of this demand over the next 25 years is real? How much of it can be done by conservation? How much can be done by co-generation? How much can be done in every way?
It goes on from there to how it can be done in an environmentally proper way. I do not think any study that could be done by this House of Commons will ever be as thorough as that study. It is going to take the next four years, but it is not dealing with the abstract. It is dealing with the power needs of the heartland of this nation, of the heartland of Ontario which is dependent on nuclear energy. If there is a better way to do it, I am sure that that royal commission will come up with it.
For this House of Commons to adopt this bill when we have a massive study, unprecedented in the history of this country, taking place in Ontario, would be pre-emptive. I would not say it would be irresponsible, but I think it would be only supernumerary to the very kind of study which is going to be done by that group which has a responsibility not just to look at the matter in abstract
Royal Assent
but to keep the power supply and the lights on and the industry in the province of Ontario operating.
I think that to pass this resolution and pre-empt something that is being done on a much larger scale and in a much more thorough way would not be in the best interests of the House or the country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to underline my total support and commitment to Canada's nuclear program.
The benefits are substantial and indeed are needed for security and diversity of energy supply. They are also needed in environmental protection and industrial development. Nuclear energy will clearly have an important role in Canada and will into the future.
Maintaining the nuclear power option is vital to our interests and vital for the society in general. What is interesting is to take a look at the western sedimentary basin which produces most of our light and medium gravity crude. Those reserves, as we are well aware, are depleting right now. We also know that oil is priced between $20 and $22 a barrel U.S. and at that price it is not economical to develop frontier and synthetic crude.
As we see our oil reserves being depleted we know that the energy supply for future development for electrical generation is very much in doubt and nuclear can play a main role.
I must add with regard to the environment that the impact of burning larger amounts of fossil fuels and the emissions that will be spewn into the air are an extreme public hazard. It also is a huge economic cost to add scrubbers to some of the large stacks that we have.
October 2, 1991

The implications are that carbon dioxide accumulation within the earth's atmosphere is extremely damaging and has the potential to change the climate.
Another thing that we all have to consider is that Canada is an industrial based country and the nuclear industry has over 30,000 people employed as a direct consequence of this industry. It is most important that- and I realize that most of these jobs are in the province of Ontario-this country maintain its industrial base and maintain the variety of sources that we have to generate electricity in this country. The Atomic Energy Control Board is the federal regulatory agency and it oversees all application development throughout this country with regard to nuclear energy.
Atomic Energy Canada Limited is the Crown owned corporation that promotes the use of nuclear energy and it is known around the world for its superb Candu reactors. They are considered the safest reactors in the world, mainly because of the containment system. It is unfair and it is misleading to compare our Candu reactor with the reactor that was in place at Chernobyl. That was a graphite based reactor and it was a man-made disaster. It is unfair and misleading to scare the people of Canada in that regard.
Private Members' Business
We know perfectly well that Canada has nuclear reactors generating electricity in Ontario and 53 per cent of Ontario's electricity is derived from nuclear energy. We also have reactors in Quebec as well as New Brunswick.
It is very, very important to look around the world. I was very fortunate to chair the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources in 1988 when we did an extremely intensive study on nuclear energy. Indeed we not only studied it in Canada and the United States but we studied it in Sweden, France and West Germany. There is no doubt about it, nuclear energy is the energy of the future and we must maintain and support Atomic Energy Canada Limited.
We cannot use tunnel vision. There is absolutely no way. We have to examine all the issues at stake. Yes, we will study it very carefully. But nuclear energy for the generation of electricity is absolutely necessary and it will go forth in Canada.
